state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think about it this way: if you had a group of toys and you cut them all in half, would the range of the sizes stay the same? Or, if you added the same amount to each toy's size, would the range change?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Hmm, so if I cut them all in half, the biggest and smallest would both get smaller by the same amount, so the gap between them would stay the same... but if I add 3 cm to each one, that would also keep the gap the same, wouldn't it? So maybe they're both right? I'm confused about why I thought only Tom was right.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you had a group of toys and you cut them all in half. Would the range of the sizes stay the same? Or, if you added the same amount to each toy's size, would the range change?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Wait, I think I see it now - if I cut them all in half, like 42 becomes 21 and 13 becomes 6.5, the difference is still 14.5, so the range stays the same. But then if I add 3 to each one, 42 becomes 45 and 13 becomes 16, so the difference is still 29... so actually both of them should be right, shouldn't they? I'm still confused about why I only picked Tom.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher fails to address the student's mathematical error (confusing halving with subtraction, and incorrectly calculating ranges), merely repeating the same generic prompt while the student arrives at an incorrect conclusion that both are right, reinforcing rather than correcting the misconception.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses a concrete, everyday analogy (toys being cut in half or growing) to help the student understand the abstract concept of range, which is a strong application of the experiential strategy, though the analogy could have been slightly more developed or varied.
